messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Arguments: Arguments, Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat

Vignette:
Amir is a 19-year-old environmental scientist, married for just over a year, who came to therapy at his wife’s gentle but persistent urging. He had not sought help before, because he did not think of himself as someone with a problem—he thought of himself as someone who had learned to be careful. The trauma that shaped that carefulness was not a single explosion of violence but a chronic, unpredictable current that ran through his childhood. His father’s physical abuse was not about punishment in any recognizable sense; it was about mood. Amir could never tell what would set it off. A question asked too late, a glass placed too loudly on the counter, a homework grade that was not bad but not good enough—anything could become the reason. The beatings themselves were not the worst part. The worst part was the silence that preceded them: the way his father would stop mid-sentence, his face going still, and Amir would know, with a sickening drop in his stomach, that something he had just done or failed to do had shifted the air. He learned to read that stillness the way a seismologist reads a fault line.

Now, at 19, Amir has built his life around the same kind of reading. He studies faces constantly—not with curiosity, but with a practiced, almost automatic vigilance. In the lab where he works, analyzing soil and water samples, he finds himself watching his colleagues’ micro-expressions during meetings, scanning for the tightening around the eyes or the flattening of the mouth that might signal impending anger. He has become expert at detecting threat in faces, but the expertise has not made him feel safer. It has only made him more exhausted. He chooses his seat in every room with care: back to the wall, full view of the door, a clear line of sight to everyone present. If he cannot sit that way, his attention fractures. He cannot focus on the data in front of him because he is too busy tracking who is approaching, who is shifting, who might be about to disagree.

Disagreement is, for Amir, a kind of trigger. Arguments of any kind—even mild differences of opinion, even a colleague saying “I see it differently”—send a current through him that feels older than his actual memory. He does not argue back. He avoids conflict entirely. He agrees too quickly, or he changes the subject, or he simply leaves the room. At work, this has made him seem agreeable but distant. His supervisor has noted that Amir rarely speaks up in team discussions, even when he clearly knows the material. At home, it is more painful. His wife, Layla, is not a confrontational person, but she is an expressive one. When she cries—over a sad movie, or a difficult phone call with her mother, or even just from exhaustion—Amir feels something close to panic. He cannot bear the sight of tears. It is not that he is unsympathetic; it is that crying, for him, signals an emotional volatility that feels dangerous. He does not know what will come next. He freezes. He leaves the room. He tells her he needs air, and then he stands outside their apartment, back against the hallway wall, breathing until the feeling passes.

He has also come to avoid being alone. The irony is not lost on him: he avoids people because he is afraid of them, and he avoids solitude because he is afraid of his own stillness. When he is alone in a room or a building, the silence feels too much like the silence before his father’s stillness. He hears things that are not there. He finds himself checking the locks, checking the corners, sitting with his back to the wall even in his own living room. So he stays near Layla. He follows her from room to room. He waits for her to come home from work. He does not tell her why, because he does not have the words, and because he is afraid that if he explains, she will see how broken he is.

The most concrete consequence of Amir’s vigilance is tactile. He cannot bear to be touched without warning. Layla learned this early in their marriage, when she came up behind him in the kitchen and placed a hand on his shoulder. He spun around, fists raised, before he even knew what he was doing. The look on her face—shock, then hurt, then fear—is something he still sees in his mind. Since then, she always announces herself. She says his name before she reaches for him. But even that is not always enough. If he is absorbed in thought, or if the light is low, a gentle touch can still send him into a full-body startle. He has come to believe that his own body is a traitor, that it will always react before his mind can catch up.

What finally brought Amir to therapy was not the avoidance, not the scanning, not the need to sit with his back to the wall. It was a moment three weeks ago, when Layla came home late from work, tired and quiet. He asked her if something was wrong. She said no. He asked again. She hesitated. In that hesitation, he saw his father’s stillness. He grabbed his keys and left the apartment, walked for two hours through the cold night, and when he came back, she was crying. He could not explain why he had left. He could not tell her that he had been certain, for a few terrible seconds, that she was about to become someone else. He is coming to therapy because he is afraid of what he will do if this keeps going. And he is afraid, too, of what it means that he cannot stop watching for danger in the face of the person he loves most.
